title: Pointers and arrays
lesson:
A plain C++ array is a row of values packed side by side in memory:

```
int readings[4] = {40, 75, 90, 20};   // a water tank sensor, 4 samples
```

The name `readings` turns into a pointer to the **first** item whenever you use it. Because the items sit next to each other, you can step through them with **pointer arithmetic**:

```
int* p = readings;   // points at 40
p + 1;               // points at 75 (one int further, not one byte)
*(p + 2);            // 90
p[2];                // exactly the same thing: p[i] means *(p + i)
```

**Passing arrays to functions.** An array passed to a function arrives as just a pointer. The function has no idea how long it is, so you must pass the length too:

```
int total(const int* values, int count)
{
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) sum += values[i];
    return sum;
}
```

The standard library often uses a **range** instead: a pointer to the first item and a pointer **one past the last**. `begin == end` means empty.

```
for (const int* p = begin; p != end; ++p) ...
```

**const and pointers.** Read the type from right to left:

- `const int* p`: a pointer to a const int. You can move `p`, but not change `*p`. Use it for "read-only input", like the sensor readings above.
- `int* const p`: a const pointer to an int. `p` always points at the same place, but you may change `*p`.
- `const int* const p`: neither.

**Why bounds matter.** C++ does not check that `p[i]` is inside the array. `readings[10]` reads whatever happens to be next in memory, or crashes, or overwrites another variable. This kind of bug, a **buffer overflow**, has caused real security holes and very confusing game crashes. The professional habit: always pass and check the length, keep loops at `i < count`, and prefer `std::vector` (with `.size()` and `.at()`) or `std::array` in new code.

Raw arrays still matter because they are what is underneath: `std::vector` keeps a pointer to a heap array, image pixels and audio samples are arrays, and Unreal's `TArray::GetData()` hands you a raw pointer for fast loops.

notes: readings turns into a pointer to its first item, so int* p = readings needs no &.
*(p + 2) and p[2] are the same: step two ints along, then read.
average takes const int* because it only reads, and a count because a pointer doesn't know its length.
readings + 1 with count 2 passes just the middle of the array: no copying.
The last loop walks a range from the first item to one past the last.

exercises.title: Sum a sensor array
exercises.prompt: Write int sumArray(const int* values, int count): the total of the first count values. A count of 0 (or less) gives 0, even if values is nullptr.

tests.hint_if_fail: Start at the pointer you are given and read count items from there.
With count 0, don't read anything at all.

hints: Loop i from 0 while i < count and add values[i].
int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) sum += values[i]; return sum;

exercises.title: Count high readings in a range
exercises.prompt: Write int countAbove(const int* begin, const int* end, int limit): how many values in the range [begin, end) are greater than limit. end points one past the last value; begin == end means an empty range.

tests.hint_if_fail: begin == end is an empty range: don't read *begin.

hints: Walk a pointer p from begin while p != end.
for (const int* p = begin; p != end; ++p) if (*p > limit) n++;

exercises.title: Reverse in place
exercises.prompt: Write void reverseInPlace(int* values, int count) that reverses the first count values in the array itself (no new array). Use two pointers that walk towards each other.

tests.call: []{ int a[] = {1, 2, 3}; reverseInPlace(a, 3); return a[0] * 100 + a[1] * 10 + a[2]; }()

tests.hint_if_fail: Only the first count values are reversed.

tests.call: []{ int a[] = {7}; reverseInPlace(a, 1); reverseInPlace(a, 0); return a[0]; }()

tests.why: Use pointers: one at the start, one at the last item.

hints: int* left = values; int* right = values + count - 1;
With count 0 or 1 there is nothing to do: return straight away.

quiz.q: int a[] = {5, 6, 7}; int* p = a; What is *(p + 1)?
quiz.why: p + 1 steps one int along, to a[1].

quiz.q: Why does sumArray(const int* values, int count) need count?
choices: A pointer doesn't know how many items follow it
quiz.why: The array becomes a bare pointer; its length is lost.

quiz.q: Which can you NOT do with const int* p?
quiz.why: It points to const ints: you can move p but not change what it points at.

quiz.q: int a[4]; a[10] = 1; What does C++ do?
choices: Nothing checks it: it may corrupt memory or crash
quiz.why: Raw arrays have no bounds checks; that's a buffer overflow.

quiz.q: In a range [begin, end), end points at...
quiz.why: One past the end, so begin == end means empty.

cards.q: const int* p vs int* const p?
cards.a: Pointer to const (can't change *p) vs const pointer (can't move p).

cards.q: Pass a raw array to a function?
cards.a: Pass a pointer and the count (or a begin/end range).

cards.q: Safer than raw arrays in new code?

explain: Explain why a function that receives an array as a pointer also needs its length, and what can go wrong without it.
